product.title: Latin 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Latin: short dialogues set in a Roman household, word-for-word translations that reveal the job of every ending, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide (classical pronunciation), exercises, and an answer key. Latin has no native speakers, yet more than half of English vocabulary comes from it — university, senate, video, audio, agenda, January. This course turns that around: from words you already know to Latin sentences you can read on your own, with all five declensions, four conjugations and six basic tenses.

blocks.text: Latin is the only language in this series with no native speakers. There's no city where people haggle over the price of fish in Latin, no small child learning to talk in it, no Latin TV show. It stopped being anyone's mother tongue some fifteen hundred years ago.

And that is exactly why it never died. For the next fifteen hundred years, Europeans kept using it for the things they considered most important: law, worship, medicine, star charts and schooling. Through the Norman French after 1066, through Renaissance scholars, and through the language of science, its words poured into English. More than half of English vocabulary comes from Latin, directly or through French — and you use hundreds of those words every day without noticing.

*Agenda* is a Latin word, whole, without a single letter changed. So are *data*, *video*, *audio*, *alibi*, *bonus*, *status*, *campus*, *exit*, *veto*. *School* comes from *schola*, *street* from *strata*, *wine* from *vinum*, *cheese* from *caseus*, and *January* from the god of doors, *Ianus*. You're not starting this language from zero. You're already carrying quite a load of supplies, and the "Words you already know" pages ahead will count them for you.

So what's genuinely new? Just one thing, but a big one: in Latin, **a word's job is decided by its ending, not by its position**. English marks who does what by word order — "the dog bites the man" is not "the man bites the dog". Latin marks it with endings, so the order is free.

blocks.text: Those four sentences hold the whole course in miniature. If you can feel why the first three mean the same and the fourth is different, you've grasped the hardest thing to explain about Latin. The rest is just lists — long lists, admittedly, but finite lists that can be learned.

There's more good news. Latin has no articles: no *the*, *a*, *der*, *le*. Its spelling is honest, one letter one sound, with no silent letters like French or English. There are no tones like Mandarin, no new alphabet to learn. And because the language no longer changes, there's no slang to make your lessons go out of date.

The tough news: Latin nouns have five groups of endings (called declensions) and its verbs have four (called conjugations). That sounds like twenty tables. In reality it's much lighter, because the groups borrow from one another: once you know the first declension, the second feels like its sibling, and the fifth is just a handful of words. This course serves them up one at a time, always after you've first met examples in a dialogue.

The dialogues are set in a Roman household in the first century: Quintus the merchant, his wife Cornelia, their children Marcus and Iulia, a teacher named Titus, and a few neighbors. The setting was chosen so that the words you learn are words that actually appear in Latin texts — *forum*, *villa*, *epistula*, *magister* — not modern terms that have to be invented.

One honest note about that setting. Rome was a conquering empire, and households like Quintus's stood on the labor of people who were not free. You'll meet the word *servus*, and in this course it is translated as it is, not softened. We learn Latin to read that world with open eyes, not to long for it.

After twenty units you'll be able to read real, unsimplified Latin sentences — from Caesar, from Seneca, from scripture, from gravestones, from university mottos. The last unit is designed for exactly that. A language that has stopped changing has one advantage no living language has: what you learn today will never go out of date.
*Incipiamus* — let's begin.

Every unit has the same structure, and there's a reason for it. You meet the language first as living sentences, and only then the explanation. Reversing that order — memorizing declension tables first — is the fastest way to make Latin feel like a punishment.
Set aside thirty to forty minutes a day. Four days in a row at half an hour each beats one whole day once a week; Latin endings stick through short, frequent repetition, not long sittings.

items: **By the end of this unit** — three things you'll be able to do once the unit is done. Read them first, and again at the end as a self-check.

**Dialogue** — twelve lines of natural conversation. Each line has three layers: the Latin, a natural translation, and a **literal** translation that unpacks the job of every ending (`girl-obj`, `see-she`). The literal layer is this course's main tool.
**Dialogue notes** — four notes that answer the questions that just popped into your head while reading the dialogue.
**Grammar sections** — two or three sections, with tables and warning boxes for the mistakes learners typically make.
**Vocabulary** — about thirty words from the unit, with a pronunciation guide and their dictionary form.
**Exercises** — four sets, twenty-four questions. Do them on paper, not in your head.
**Answer key** — on the following page. Check yourself, and if you got something wrong, find the dialogue line that contains the pattern.

blocks.title: How to read the literal translation
items: Hyphens attach information that Latin carries in the word's own ending. *Puellam* → `girl-obj`. *Puellae* → `girl-of`. *Videt* → `see-she`.

The labels used throughout the course: the subject (who acts) is left plain, **-obj** (what the action is done to), **-of** (possession or "of"), **-to** (the receiver or goal), **-with** / **-in** / **-from** (means, place, origin), and **-call** (the person being addressed). Also **-pl** (plural), **-masc** / **-fem** / **-neut** (gender), **-Q** (the question marker *-ne*), and **-was** / **-did** / **-will** for past and future verbs.
A subject with a plain ending gets no label at all, so the line doesn't fill up with tags. So `girl see-she boy-obj` means the girl is the one doing it.
The literal translation is deliberately awkward. If it read naturally, it would fail to show how Latin builds its sentences.

blocks.title: Why this course prints pronunciation instead of providing audio
items: Latin has no recordings of native speakers, and no AI voice reads it with correct classical pronunciation. So this course doesn't offer tap-to-listen like the living-language courses — instead you get a **Say it** column in every vocabulary row.
Read the dialogues aloud. Latin was written to be spoken; its sentences are built with rhythm, and that rhythm only comes alive in your own mouth.

A bar over a vowel (*a*, *e*, *i*, *o*, *u* become ā, ē, ī, ō, ū) marks a long vowel — held about twice as long. The Romans themselves never wrote it, and this course doesn't use it, so the text looks like the Latin you'll meet in the wild. What the Say-it column marks is the stress: the syllable in capital letters is said louder and slightly longer.

blocks.title: If you only have ten minutes today
items: Read the dialogue aloud once all the way through, without stopping at words you don't know.
Read it again, following the literal layer.
Close the book. Tomorrow, start with the dialogue notes. Ten minutes actually done beat an hour only planned.

blocks.text: The names of the months — and a little puzzle

All twelve of our month names are Roman month names, almost unchanged: *Ianuarius, Februarius, Martius, Aprilis, Maius, Iunius, Iulius, Augustus, September, October, November, December*. The last four contain Latin numbers: *septem* seven, *octo* eight, *novem* nine, *decem* ten. Yet September is the ninth month, not the seventh.

The reason: the Roman year originally began in March. September really was the seventh month — until Ianuarius and Februarius were slipped in at the front and pushed everything along. The numbers were never fixed, and we still use them today. Latin hides a great many things like this, and that's what makes it fun.

blocks.title: Careful: false friends
items: *Vir* isn't "virus" — it means "man" (think *virile*). *Virus* is a Latin word too, but it means "poison, slime".
*Amare* means "to love"; it's the parent of *amateur* — someone who does something for love, not for pay.

*Familia* in Latin isn't the "nuclear family" but **the whole household**, including the workers and unfree people in it. It's one example of a word whose form survived while its content changed completely.
A *villa* isn't a luxury holiday home; in Latin it's a farmhouse outside town.

blocks.text: The good news first: Latin is written exactly as it sounds, one letter one sound, with no silent letters. There are five vowels — a, e, i, o, u — and all five are pure, steady sounds like the vowels of Spanish or Italian, never the gliding vowels of English (Latin *o* is not "oh-oo").

This course uses **classical pronunciation**, the way the Romans themselves sounded their language in the time of Caesar and Cicero. Another way of reading is still alive today, the church (ecclesiastical) pronunciation, which follows the sounds of Italian; the differences are summed up in the last table of this section. Both are legitimate. Pick one and stay consistent. How to read the **Say it** column: **ah** as in *father*, **eh** as in *bed*, **ee** as in *see*, **i** as in *sit*, **oh** a pure o as in *more* (no "w" at the end), **oo** as in *food*; **eye**/**ye** as in *eye*, *bye*; **ow** as in *how*; **oy** as in *boy*; **ay** as in *day*. **g** is always hard as in *get*, even before e and i (GIN as in *begin*); **s** is always as in *sun*; **w** and **y** as in *wet*, *yes*. Capital letters mark the stressed syllable.
The three letters people get wrong most

Those three letters alone separate someone who's learning Latin from someone who's just spelling out Latin letters. *Caesar* is pronounced **KYE-sahr** — which is where German *Kaiser* and Russian *tsar* come from — not the English "SEE-zer".

blocks.text: Double vowels

*Ae* is Latin's calling card, and it turns up everywhere: the ending *-ae* on feminine nouns marks the "of" form, the "to" form and the plural all at once. Reading it **eye** from day one will save you a lot of confusion later.
Which syllable is stressed
Latin has a stress rule with almost no exceptions, and it fits in two lines. Count syllables from the end.

head: Number of syllables
Stressed syllable
Examples

blocks.text: A syllable counts as long if its vowel is long, if it's a double vowel, or if two consonants follow it. Because vowel length isn't written, the **Say it** column in every vocabulary list marks the stressed syllable in capitals. Just follow that column, and in time your ear will guess on its own.
If you've heard a different pronunciation

blocks.title: Five mistakes English speakers make most often
items: Reading *c* as "s". In Latin it's **always k**: *cena* = KEH-nah, *Cicero* = KEE-keh-roh, not "SIS-er-oh".
Reading *v* as "v". It's **w**: *vinum* = WEE-noom. The Romans even wrote it with the same letter as U.
Swallowing endings into a vague "uh". The endings carry the meaning; *puella*, *puellam* and *puellae* make three different sentences. Sound every vowel fully, right to the last letter.
Reading *ae* as "ee", the way English says *Caesar* or *alumnae*. It's **eye**: *Caesar* = KYE-sahr, *puellae* = poo-EHL-lye.
Stressing the last syllable, or stressing by English habit. In Latin the last syllable of a longer word is **never** stressed: *amicus* = ah-MEE-koos, not "AM-i-cus".

blocks.text: That last sentence isn't decoration. Latin really does belong to those willing to repeat: one declension table read five times over five days sticks far better than fifty times in one night.

If you've reached this page and the Unit 20 exercises made sense, you're past the steepest part. You know five declensions, four conjugations, six tenses, and enough vocabulary to read short sentences without a dictionary. By CEFR standards, that's a full A1.
What hasn't been taught here

items: **The subjunctive** — verb forms for wishes, purposes and hypotheticals (*ut veniat*, "so that he may come"). It's the core of the next level.
**Participles and the ablative absolute** — Latin's way of squeezing a whole clause into two words (*urbe capta*, "once the city was taken").
**Indirect statement with accusative and infinitive** — *dicit puellam venire*, "he says that the girl is coming".
**The pluperfect and future perfect** in full, along with the whole passive system in the past tenses.
**Gerunds and gerundives**, and Roman numerals in more complex use.

blocks.text: How to keep going, starting today

items: **Read graded texts.** The most powerful way to strengthen A1 isn't memorizing new tables but reading hundreds of easy sentences. Look for beginner Latin readers written entirely in Latin, with pictures; "read a lot, look up a little" is the proven fastest route.

**Start with the friendliest original texts.** The Vulgate Gospels, Aesop's fables in Latin, and Seneca's short letters are written in far straighter sentences than Cicero. Caesar is famously clear too, even if his sentences are long.
**Write three sentences a day.** About the weather, what you ate, what you're working on. Three sentences a day for a month make endings stick better than twenty pages of exercises.
**Read aloud.** With no native speakers to correct you, your own mouth becomes your teacher. The rhythm of a Latin sentence is part of its meaning.

**Collect inscriptions.** University mottos, writing on old buildings, scientific names of plants, sentences on coins. Finding a Latin sentence out in the real world and being able to read it yourself is a reward no other language gives.

blocks.text: And if one day you stand in front of an old building, read a line carved two thousand years ago, and understand it with no one in between — that's the whole reason this language is still taught. *Macte virtute*: keep it up.
